## PURPOSE

The purpose is to defend structured-output APIs against control-plane jailbreaks (where malicious instructions are embedded in JSON schema forced literals) without model retraining or inference overhead.

Looking through the papers: Papers [1], [4], [6], [9], [11], [13] address jailbreak defenses generally, but none specifically target the control-plane / structured-output API attack vector. Papers [5], [7], [8], [10], [20], [23] address prompt injection defenses, which is a related but distinct threat model (data-plane injection vs. schema-level control-plane attack). None of these papers address the specific gap of defending against jailbreaks embedded in JSON schema definitions/forced literals. The closest is [5] ("Context-Aware Token Sanitization" for prompt injection in LLM APIs), but prompt injection in web APIs is not the same as schema-level control-plane jailbreaks in structured-output APIs. No prior paper closes the same gap.

## MECHANISM

The mechanism is a training-free schema sanitizer that flags suspicious forced literals via a conjunction-based heuristic (long values, whitespace, imperative verbs) and replaces them with opaque placeholders preserving schema structure.

Paper [3] performs text sanitization by replacing sensitive entities with substitutes, but targets privacy/PII, not security jailbreaks in schemas. Paper [17] ("Pr????mpt") sanitizes sensitive prompts by replacing sensitive tokens with placeholders — this is structurally similar (replace suspicious tokens with placeholders), but the purpose is privacy protection of user prompts, not schema sanitization for jailbreak defense. Paper [5] mentions "context-aware token sanitization" for prompt injection. Paper [23] (PromptArmor) detects and removes injected prompts. Paper [26] (Februus) sanitizes inputs by removing trigger artifacts. None of these use a conjunction-based heuristic on schema structure (long values + whitespace + imperative verbs) to sanitize JSON schema forced literals specifically. The closest primitive is placeholder substitution in [17] and [3], but the specific mechanism of heuristic-flagging of schema fields and replacing with opaque placeholders while preserving schema structure is not covered. The CDR papers [28], [30] do "disarm and reconstruct" files by removing malicious content while preserving structure — this is conceptually similar (remove threat, preserve structure). Paper [30] explicitly describes CDR as "proactively extracts threat attack vectors from documents... preserving the file's usability." This is the same underlying primitive: identify and neutralize malicious embedded content while preserving the container structure.

## EVALUATION

The evaluation uses HarmBench attack success rate (ASR) as the metric, tested on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B, with a benign schema modification rate as a false-positive metric.

HarmBench is a named benchmark family used in prior work. Paper [11] explicitly mentions "HarmBench" — "exceeding 70% attack success rate (ASR) on HarmBench against defenses." Paper [2] uses ASR as a metric for jailbreak evaluation. The evaluation design (ASR on HarmBench, tested on LLMs) is covered by [11].

## DOMAIN

The domain is LLM security / structured-output APIs. Papers [1], [2], [4], [6], [9], [11], [13], [14] all work in LLM security/jailbreak defense. This is clearly covered.
